cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-vision-of-.summary: Within a golden medallion at the top of the page Christ sits enthroned and blessing, while six-winged seraphim and ranks of angels holding staffs fill the sky beneath him; at the left the prophet Isaiah, labelled, reels back in awe. The inscription names the scene as the vision of Isaiah, in which the Lord appears 'sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up'. Byzantine artists showed the Lord of the vision with the features of Christ.
facts: The heading at the top left reads 'Vision of Isaiah' (ΟΡΑΣΙΣ ΗΣΑΙΟΥ).
Many of its full-page miniatures do not illustrate Gregory's sermons directly but set biblical and historical scenes beside them as a commentary devised for the court.
cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-vision-of-.notes: Folio derived from the Gallica image sequence (view number minus 13, halved) and checked against folios named on other Commons files of this manuscript; the Commons file name gives the Gallica view number, not the folio. The lower register is badly damaged.

cur:manuscripts-valcavado-praise-of-the-.summary: Above, the haloed Lord sits enthroned and blessing between the four winged living creatures; beneath him the twenty-four elders lie prostrate in worship in layered rows, and in the lowest band John falls at the feet of an angel. The caption reads 'where the four living creatures and the elders adore the throne'.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.

Q116243170.summary: Along this long marble lid a young shepherd, Christ, stands at the centre between two flocks: sheep crowd in from the left under leafy trees, and goats press in from the right, framed by fluted shell-like ornaments at each end. Carved for a Christian burial, it gives quiet form to Christ's words about the Last Judgement, when the Son of Man will separate the sheep from the goats.
facts: The lid is about 2.37 m long and weighs about 103 kg; the Met acquired it through the Rogers Fund in 1924.
Early Christian art often expressed the Last Judgement through Christ's parable of the sheep and the goats, long before the later type of Christ enthroned as judge became common.
Q116243170.notes: The Met's date carries a question mark: 'late 3rd–early 4th century (?)'.

walters:71.158.summary: In the central panel of this small ivory triptych the Virgin holds the Christ Child on her left arm and points to him with her right hand; the Child, with a cross-nimbus, blesses and holds a scroll. Beneath a pierced arch, mother and Son face the viewer, while on the wings two pairs of saints, one above the other, turn to them in homage. Traces of pigment and gold show that it was once brightly painted.
facts: The Virgin's pose is the Hodegetria, named after a famous icon in the Hodegon monastery in Constantinople that was believed in the Middle Ages to have been painted by St Luke.
The Walters notes that the panels were cut down and do not align perfectly, so the triptych may have been assembled from two earlier pieces.
It was once given by Bishop Heinrich von Hofstätter of Passau to the Gnadenkapelle at Altötting in Bavaria (1867).

Q2182509.summary: The risen Christ stands with the cross, the reed and the sponge — the instruments of his Passion — held lightly against his body, turning his head away in a powerful spiral movement. Michelangelo presents him as a perfect, heroic nude, his triumph over death expressed through the beauty of the human form. It stands beside the high altar of Rome's great Gothic Dominican church.
facts: Michelangelo abandoned a first version when a black vein appeared in the marble across Christ's face; that earlier statue was rediscovered in a church at Bassano Romano and identified in 2000.
The finishing of the second version in Rome was entrusted to his assistant Pietro Urbano, who damaged it and was replaced by Federico Frizzi.
The bronze loincloth was added in 1546, in keeping with changing standards of decorum.
